division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.53(1)  The Court may give judgment against a third party
defendant if the third party defendant does not file a statement of
defence.
(2)  Judgment against a defendant must be satisfied before
judgment is enforced against a third party defendant unless the
Court otherwise orders.
(3)  An application by a defendant to enforce a judgment against a
third party defendant under subrule (2) must
(a) be in Form 19, and
(b) be served on the plaintiff and the third party defendant.

BOOK_B.title: Judgment against third party defendant

commentary.text: Rule 3.53 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.53. 1. Deemed admissions In Melcosky v. Maguire, 2015 ABQB 434, the third party was noted in default. Justice Read said: 108 When a party is noted in default, the claims are deemed to have been admitted and all that may be controverted is the amount of the judgment (Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7 (at para 5). The amount of the judgment must be assessed unless the claim is for a debt or liquidated demand (r 3.39). In Yaremchuk v. Haight, 2001 ABCA 7, the Court said: 5 In my view, a party who is noted in default does not cease to be a party to the action and is entitled to utilize Rule 244.1. According to Rule 142(3) once a defendant has been noted in default he or she is no longer entitled to deliver a statement of defence or demand of notice. Furthermore, once the defendant has been noted in default: • [a]ll the plaintiff has to prove, or the defendant is permitted to controvert, is the amount of the damages; for the cause of action itself, as stated in the plaintiff's claim, and the right to some damages in respect of it, is admitted by the defendant, by his suffering judgement to pass against him by default. • T.W. Chitty, ed., Chitty's Archibold's Practice of the Queen's Bench Division, vol. 2, 14th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1885) at 1336, as cited in Sulef v. Parkin and Breno (1966), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.) But I have not been provided with any authority or directed to any Rule which might otherwise limit the right of a defendant to take any other step under the Rules. 2. Setting aside on failure to defend The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, in interpreting the equivalent rule, set out several principles for setting aside the default: The general principles governing the right to set aside a default judgment apply. Lamont, J.A. (as he then was) set out these principles in Klein v. Schile, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 78, at page 79, as follows: The circumstances under which a Court will exercise its discretion to set aside a judgment regularly signed are pretty well settled. The application should be made as soon as possible after the judgment comes to the knowledge of the defendant, but more delay will not bar the application, unless an irreparable injury will be done to the plaintiff or the delay has been wilful … The application should be supported by an affidavit setting out the circumstances under which the default arose and disclosing a defence on the merits … It is not sufficient to merely state that the defendant has a good defence upon the merits. The affidavits must show the nature of the defence and set forth facts which will enable the Court or Judge to decide whether or not there was matter which would afford a defence to the action … If the application is not made immediately after the defendant has become aware that judgment has been signed against him, the affidavits should also explain the delay in making the application; and, if that delay be of long standing, the defence on the merits must be clearly established. Warner Construction Co. v. Wood River (Rural Municipality) (1979), 1 Sask. R. 118 at 119-20 (C.A.).
